questions.prompt: A city library offers a new late-return text alert. Members opt in at the desk. After three months, members with the alert return 12 points more books on time than members without it. What kind of study is this?
options: A randomised experiment, because two groups are compared
A quasi-experiment, because the alert started on a fixed date
An observational comparison, because members chose the alert
A lottery, because not every member received the alert
misconceptions: Takes any two-group comparison for an experiment: what matters is how the groups were formed
Sees a date and assumes a rule created the groups: here members chose
Confuses partial coverage with assignment by chance
questions.explanation: Members decided for themselves whether to opt in, so the two groups may differ in many ways besides the alert. That is an observational comparison.

questions.prompt: A transport office finds that drivers who use its mobile app renew their licences on time 20 points more often than drivers who do not. A simulation shows that conscientious drivers both install the app more and renew on time more. What does the 20-point gap mostly measure?
options: The difference between conscientious drivers and the others
The effect of the app on every driver who installs it
The sampling error of a survey of drivers
The effect of on-time renewal on app use
misconceptions: Reads a gap between groups that chose as the effect of the thing they chose
Mistakes a stable bias for noise: a larger survey would show the same gap
Reverses the direction without removing the hidden trait that drives both
questions.explanation: A trait that drives both app use and renewal is mixed into the comparison. The gap is mostly that trait, not the app.

questions.prompt: Three separate surveys of clinic patients all find that patients who booked online miss fewer appointments, by 9, 10 and 11 points. A manager says the agreement proves that online booking reduces missed appointments. What is the best reply?
options: Three surveys are too few; ten would settle it
The surveys share one weakness: patients chose how to book
The surveys disagree by 2 points, so none can be trusted
The effect is real, since chance cannot produce it three times
misconceptions: Treats bias as noise that more studies average away
Reads ordinary sampling variation as a contradiction
Rules out chance and forgets that a shared bias repeats just as reliably
questions.explanation: Agreement between studies that share the same bias shows that the bias is stable, not that the claim is true. All three compare patients who chose.

questions.prompt: A municipality waives a parking fee for cars registered before 2015. An analyst compares permit renewals of cars registered in late 2014 with cars registered in early 2015. On which assumption does a causal reading rest?
options: That the two groups have the same number of cars
That owners chose their registration year at random
That renewals were measured in the same month for all cars
That nothing else changes at the 2015 line besides the fee
misconceptions: Looks for equal group sizes, which matter for precision and not for the causal claim
Asks for randomisation, which a rule at a cut-off does not need or provide
Names a measurement detail in place of the assumption the design rests on
questions.explanation: A comparison just either side of a cut-off supports a causal claim if units near the line are alike and nothing else switches at the line.

questions.prompt: A housing office has 300 places on a home-repair scheme and 1,400 eligible applicants. Places are allocated by a recorded random draw. One year later, energy bills of the two groups are compared. Which claim does the comparison support?
options: The scheme lowered bills for applicants like these
The scheme lowers bills for every household in the city
Households on the scheme have lower bills; the reason is unknown
The scheme lowers bills only if bills were moving in parallel before
misconceptions: Extends the result beyond the units that were in the draw
Treats a lottery as an observational comparison because nobody planned a study
Borrows the assumption of a before-and-after comparison that a random draw does not need
questions.explanation: A recorded random draw is random assignment. It supports a causal claim for the applicants who were in the draw.

questions.prompt: A health centre knows from strong earlier trials that a reminder call reduces missed vaccinations. A manager proposes a new test in which half of the parents get no call, to measure the effect locally. What is the main objection?
options: The test would need too many parents to reach significance
The local effect cannot differ from the earlier trials
Half of the parents would be denied a benefit already shown to work
Parents cannot be randomised without written consent in every case
misconceptions: Raises a size question when the problem is whether the test should be run at all
Assumes that results transfer exactly, which is a separate and weaker point
States a blanket rule the scenario does not give
questions.explanation: Withholding is acceptable when nobody knows whether the change helps. Here the benefit is established, so a no-call arm denies a known benefit.

questions.prompt: Four teams wrote the decision line of a pre-registration for a new queue ticket. Which line gives the director a rule she can apply on the last day?
options: We will learn whether the new ticket improves the visitor experience
If waits fall by at least 2 minutes and complaints do not rise, we adopt it
If the result is significant we adopt the ticket in all branches
We adopt the ticket unless the test shows that it is harmful
misconceptions: States curiosity, not a decision: no action follows from any result
Ties the decision to significance, which says nothing about whether the gain is large enough
Decides in advance: the test can only confirm what was going to happen anyway
questions.explanation: A decision line names the action for each result and contains the number that separates them.

questions.prompt: A text reminder costs 0.30 riyals per resident. Each missed bulky-waste collection costs the city 15 riyals. By how many points must the reminder reduce missed collections to pay for itself?
questions.explanation: Break-even is the cost per resident over the cost of one miss: 0.30 / 15 = 0.02, which is 2 points.

questions.prompt: On-time payment is 40%. A report says a new letter raised it 'by 5%'. A colleague reads this as 45%, another as 42%. Which wording removes the doubt?
options: It raised on-time payment by 5 per cent of payers
It raised on-time payment significantly, by 5%
It raised on-time payment by roughly a twentieth
It raised on-time payment by 5 points, from 40% to 45%
misconceptions: Keeps the ambiguous word and adds a second ambiguity
Adds a statistical word that does not say which 5% is meant
Chooses the relative reading without saying so
questions.explanation: 'Points' names the difference between two percentages, and giving both rates leaves no room for the relative reading.

questions.prompt: A tax office tests a firmer payment letter. Which of these is a complete guardrail?
options: We will monitor complaints closely throughout the test
Complaints must not rise; if they do, we will discuss it
If the complaint rate exceeds control by 1 point, pause and review the letter
Complaints are a secondary metric and will be reported
misconceptions: Names a metric without a threshold or an action
Has no number, so 'rise' will be argued about afterwards
Confuses a metric that explains with one that can stop the test
questions.explanation: A guardrail has a metric, a threshold and the action taken when the threshold is crossed.

questions.prompt: A utility tests two versions of its bill. Its system tosses a coin for every bill printed. One customer in four has several meters and gets several bills. What goes wrong?
options: Customers with several meters see both versions, so the arms contaminate each other
The arms will have unequal numbers of bills
Bills cannot be analysed because they are not people
The test will need four times as many bills
misconceptions: Expects a coin per bill to unbalance the counts, which it does not
Rejects the row as a unit for the wrong reason
Invents a size penalty where the problem is who receives which version
questions.explanation: A person who receives both versions is in both arms. The unit must be the customer, so that every bill of a customer lands in one arm.

questions.prompt: A school district wants to test a new homework platform. Pupils in a class work together and share one teacher. Three pairs of small schools share their teaching staff. What should be randomised?
options: Pupils, since there are far more of them
Classes, since pupils in a class share a teacher
Schools, treating each pair that shares staff as one unit
Homework tasks, since the platform logs each task
misconceptions: Picks the unit with the most rows and ignores that classmates affect each other
Stops one level too low: teachers shared between schools carry the platform across
Takes the row of the log for the unit
questions.explanation: Whatever shares staff must land in one arm together. Schools are the unit, and schools that share teachers count as one.

questions.prompt: A test of a new counter routine logs 14,400 visits in 30 branches. Four pairs of branches share staff and each pair is treated as one unit. How many units does the test have?
questions.explanation: Four pairs become four units in place of eight branches: 30 − 4 = 26. The 14,400 visits are rows, not units.

questions.prompt: A pre-registration says holders will be 'analysed as assigned'. During the test, 4% of the reminder arm never receive the reminder because of a system fault. How are these holders treated in the analysis?
options: They are moved to the control arm, since they got no reminder
They are removed, since they did not receive the treatment
They are analysed separately as a third arm
They stay in the reminder arm, where the coin put them
misconceptions: Regroups by what happened, which breaks the comparability the coin created
Drops units from one arm only, and those units are not a random handful
Creates a group that chance did not assign
questions.explanation: Analysis as assigned keeps every unit in the arm that chance chose. It estimates the effect of deciding to send reminders, failures included.

questions.prompt: A team pre-registered completion as the primary metric of a form test. Halfway through, an analyst proposes to add time on page as a further metric. What is the sound way to do it?
options: Replace completion with time on page if it shows a clearer result
Add it with a date and report it as exploratory
Add it and treat both as primary
Refuse: nothing may be added after the start
misconceptions: Lets the data choose the metric that decides
Doubles the chances of a win after seeing interim data
Reads the page as a ceiling when it is a floor
questions.explanation: Additions after the start are allowed when dated and labelled exploratory. What decides, when the test stops and who counts may not change.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of designing a test in the order in which they should be settled.
options: Write the decision the result will change
Choose one primary metric and its minimum effect
Choose the unit of randomisation
Compute the sample size and the duration
Have someone else review the page
Assign the first unit
questions.explanation: The decision comes first because everything else serves it; the metric and minimum effect come before the size because the size depends on them; the review comes before the first unit is assigned, never after.

questions.prompt: A city tests a new recycling leaflet at a 5% significance level with 80% power for a 3-point effect. In truth the leaflet raises recycling by exactly 3 points. How often will a test of this design fail to show a significant result?
options: About 5 times in 100
About 20 times in 100
About 80 times in 100
Never, because the effect is real
misconceptions: Uses the significance level, which describes the case where there is no effect
Takes the power for the chance of missing the effect
Assumes that a real effect always shows, as if samples did not vary
questions.explanation: Power of 80% means that a real effect of the stated size is found 80 times in 100 and missed 20 times.

questions.prompt: A test needs 5,000 customers per arm to detect an effect of 4 points. The manager decides that 2 points would already justify the change. How many customers per arm does the test need now, to the nearest thousand?
questions.explanation: The effect is squared in the denominator of the sample-size formula. Half the effect needs four times the size: 4 × 5,000 = 20,000.

questions.prompt: Two offices plan the same test with the same minimum effect of 2 points. Office A has a baseline of 50%, office B a baseline of 90%. Which office needs more people per arm, and why?
options: Office B, because a high baseline leaves less room to improve
Both need the same, because the minimum effect is the same
Office B, because 2 points is a smaller share of 90%
Office A, because a yes-or-no outcome is noisiest near 50%
misconceptions: Reasons about ceilings and not about the variance of the outcome
Forgets that the spread of a yes-or-no outcome depends on its rate
Thinks in relative terms when the test is planned in points
questions.explanation: The variance p(1 − p) is 0.25 at 50% and 0.09 at 90%. More noise needs more people for the same difference in points.

questions.prompt: A test needs 7,200 applicants per arm, and both arms fill from the same stream. The service receives 900 applicants a day on average. How many days of average traffic fill the test?
questions.explanation: Both arms together need 14,400 applicants. At 900 a day that is 16 days.

questions.prompt: An analyst simulates a planned test 400 times and finds a power of 77%. The formula gave 80%. Two standard errors of a share near 0.8 counted over 400 runs are about 4 points. What should she conclude?
options: The formula is wrong and the test needs more people
The simulation is wrong, since it disagrees with the formula
The two agree within the simulation's own error
The power is exactly 77%, since a simulation uses real draws
misconceptions: Reads a difference inside the counting error as a real disagreement
Treats the formula as the truth and the simulation as its imitation
Forgets that a count over 400 runs is itself an estimate
questions.explanation: 77% and 80% differ by 3 points, less than the counting error of 4. To tighten the comparison she can run more simulated tests.

questions.prompt: A team will analyse its test with a t-test on the mean rating per clinic. To check the power by simulation, what must the simulated analysis be?
options: The same t-test on clinic means, run on simulated clinics
A z-test on all patients, because it has more rows
Whichever test gives the highest simulated power
No test: the simulated effect is compared with the true effect
misconceptions: Simulates a different analysis from the one that will be run
Chooses the analysis by its result, which is what a plan is meant to prevent
Checks the estimate's accuracy and not how often the planned test detects the effect
questions.explanation: A power simulation rehearses the analysis that will really be run, at the unit that will really be analysed.

questions.prompt: In a test that randomises health centres, the intraclass correlation of the outcome is 0.02 and each centre contributes 201 patients. What is the design effect?
questions.explanation: Design effect = 1 + (m − 1) × ICC = 1 + 200 × 0.02 = 5. The variance of the estimate is five times that of a patient-randomised test of the same size.

questions.prompt: A test randomises 20 post offices, 10 per arm, and its simulated power is 35%. The team can afford one of four changes. Which one raises the power most?
options: Doubling the number of customers surveyed in each office
Analysing customers one by one in place of office averages
Raising the significance level's precision to four decimals
Adding 20 more post offices to the test
misconceptions: Shrinks only the sampling part of each office's rate; the difference between offices stays
Inflates false wins and does not add information
Changes how a number is printed, not what the data can show
questions.explanation: In a cluster-randomised test the number of clusters is the main lever. More customers per office hardly help once each office's rate is measured well.

questions.prompt: A test randomised 24 branches and found no difference in branch averages (p = 0.40). A second analyst reanalyses the 11,000 visits as independent observations and reports p = 0.001. Which analysis should the office trust?
options: The visit-level one, because 11,000 observations beat 24
The branch-level one, because branches were randomised
Neither, because two analyses of one test must agree
The visit-level one, because its p-value is smaller
misconceptions: Counts rows as units: visits in one branch are not independent
Expects agreement between a valid and an invalid analysis
Chooses the analysis by its result
questions.explanation: The unit of analysis must be the unit of randomisation. The visit-level test treats luck in which branches landed where as an effect; in simulation it declares a win most of the time when nothing differs.

questions.prompt: Before randomising 18 libraries, a team sorts them by last year's lending rate, pairs neighbours in the list and tosses a coin inside each pair. Why does this raise the power of the test?
options: It doubles the number of libraries in the analysis
It guarantees that the treated libraries perform better
It removes stable differences between libraries from the comparison
It lets the team choose which library of a pair is treated
misconceptions: Thinks pairing adds units; it adds none
Mistakes a design that removes noise for one that creates an effect
Forgets the coin: a chosen assignment would bring bias back
questions.explanation: Libraries in a pair started at the same level, so the comparison inside pairs is free of the stable differences between libraries, which are most of the noise.

questions.prompt: A test of a booking page starts on a Sunday. Weekend traffic is half of weekday traffic, and bookings surge in the last four days of each month. The planned sample size is reached on day 10, which is the 12th of the month. Which duration should the team choose?
options: 10 days, since the size is reached
14 days, two whole weeks
21 days, three whole weeks
28 days, four whole weeks
misconceptions: Stops at the size and leaves some weekdays counted twice and others once
Covers whole weeks and misses the month-end surge
Ends on the 23rd, before the surge starts
questions.explanation: The run should cover whole weeks and the month-end. From the 3rd, 28 days reach the 30th and include the surge; 21 days end on the 23rd.

questions.prompt: Two teams test the same reminder for 8 days each. Team A, in the first half of the month, estimates +1.8 points. Team B, at the month-end, estimates +3.3 points. Both tests are sound. What is the most likely reason for the gap?
options: One team made an error in its analysis
Each test estimates the effect for the days it covered
Team B had more people and so a larger effect
The reminder got better between the two tests
misconceptions: Assumes that two correct tests must give the same number
Confuses the precision of an estimate with its size
Invents a change in the treatment to explain a difference in the window
questions.explanation: If a reminder helps more in the month-end rush, a test that covers only part of the monthly cycle estimates the effect for that part.

questions.prompt: A test sends notices for 28 days. The primary metric is renewal by the expiry date, which is 30 days after each notice. An analyst wants to report the result on day 29. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing: all notices have been sent
The sample ratio cannot be checked until day 58
The test should have stopped at day 9 instead
Holders notified late have not yet reached their expiry date
misconceptions: Takes the end of sending for the end of the outcome
Ties a check on assignment to the outcome window, which it does not need
Returns to the sample size and ignores the question asked
questions.explanation: The metric is complete for a holder only at the expiry date. The last holders reach it 30 days after the last notice.
